<reason>PRO (A) controlled the decisive clash from Rebuttal 1 onward: A2.1 turned CON's own examples (address, seat, party size) into proof that mandatory fees are determined before checkout, forcing CON to retreat to edge cases. CON's counter-list leaned on optional items (tips, promos, upsells), which A3's Q1 exposed; CON's genuine examples (card surcharges, surge fees) arrived fully only in Rebuttal 2 and were adequately answered (published schedule; sliver needing tailoring). A also won the blending clash — total-vs-total comparison matches the motion's core demand, and A's own opening example treated the all-in price as the honest comparator, defusing B4.4's "itemization" overclaim. The cancel-button/abandonment point was cleanly reversed ("a trap some victims escape is still a trap"). CON's closing landed a real textualist point on "all" and the carve-out, but B4.5's concession that knowable fees are already disclosed "close enough to matter" both conceded PRO's principle and rested on an empirical claim A5.1 credibly demolished, and CON never defended it. Execution costs on both sides: CON's clipped opening killed its small-business burden argument; A4.3 misdescribed B2.1's list and claimed CON "went quiet" before CON's answer turn. Net: A answered the most important pressure more directly and framed the choice (moment of decision vs. maximum lock-in) more memorably across every round.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A2.1's capture of CON's opening concession — that fees depend on address and seat, inputs supplied before checkout — reframed the entire debate and reduced CON's structural objection to edge cases; A5.1's demolition of B4.5's "disclosure already happens" concession sealed it.</best_rebuttal>
